DEPENDENCY CONFUSION CHECK · RUNS IN YOUR BROWSER

Could a public package be substituted for your internal one?

In 2021, researcher Alex Birsan got code execution inside Apple, Microsoft, PayPal, Netflix, Uber, and Tesla by publishing decoy packages under their internal package names on the public npm and PyPI registries. Two configuration shapes made every one of those incidents possible: pip --extra-index-url, which lets a public index outbid your private one on version number, and an unscoped npm dependency name, which falls back to the public registry the moment your private .npmrc is not in effect. Paste your config below and find both, each with the exact fix.

Nothing is uploaded. What you paste is read in this browser and never leaves your device, and this tool makes no network calls of its own — it never queries npm or PyPI on your behalf.

1. Paste your config

Any of the four boxes can be left empty — the check only runs on what you provide.

Paste at least one file above and click Check.

Prefer a CLI, or want this in your own CI?

Same logic, zero dependencies, one file:

python3 check.py                  # scan a repository checkout
python3 check.py /path/to/repo    # scan a specific checkout
python3 check.py --format json    # machine-readable
python3 check.py --fail-on-risk   # exit 2 if any finding exists

Get check.py from the repo — stdlib only, nothing to install, no network calls. Wire --fail-on-risk into your own CI to block a newly-added finding before it merges.

Already running a registry-aware supply-chain platform like Socket? See how this checker differs — different layers, worth running both.

Been grepping your own requirements.txt and package.json for these patterns by hand? See what a manual check structurally can't catch.

Common questions

What is dependency confusion?

In 2021, researcher Alex Birsan demonstrated that many companies' internal build tooling would install a same-named public package instead of their own internal one, and got code execution inside Apple, Microsoft, PayPal, Netflix, Uber, Tesla and others by publishing decoy packages under their internal package names on the public npm and PyPI registries.

How does pip --extra-index-url cause this?

pip's own documentation names this as a risk: the additional repository named by --extra-index-url can specify a version of a package that gets installed instead of the one from --index-url, because pip compares versions across every configured index and installs whichever reports the higher number for a given name. A public package published under your internal package's name, at a higher version, wins.

How does an unscoped npm name cause this?

When a repository's .npmrc sets a bare registry= to a private host, that value is the default for every unscoped dependency, public or internal. A machine or CI runner without that .npmrc in effect resolves the same unscoped name against the public npm registry instead — and if nobody has claimed it there, an attacker can.

Does this tool check whether a name is actually claimed on the public registry?

No. It makes no network calls at all. It flags every unscoped dependency once a private registry is configured, including ones that are already legitimately public — a dependency on left-pad looks identical, from a read-only view of package.json, to an internal package of the same shape. Read each flagged name yourself and judge which ones you actually intend to keep private.

Does a clean scan mean I am not exposed to dependency confusion?

No. This checks two specific, well-documented configuration patterns. It is not a security audit and makes no claim about your overall supply-chain exposure. It does not parse Pipfile, poetry.lock, pnpm-lock.yaml, or yarn.lock, and it does not recurse into a monorepo's per-package manifests.

More: what is dependency confusion?

vs-checking-configs-by-hand.html.text:
← Dependency Confusion Check

This tool vs. checking pip/npm configs by hand

Names no specific company or product — this compares against the manual habit most developers already have: grepping requirements.txt or pip.conf for --extra-index-url, and skimming package.json for a dependency name that looks like it should be internal.

What checking by hand actually does

Grepping your own config is free and needs no tool, which is exactly why it is the default. You search requirements.txt or pip.conf for the string --extra-index-url, and you scan package.json's dependency names for anything that looks like it should be an internal package rather than a public one.

That method has failure modes specific to this domain that this tool exists to close. First, knowing to search for --extra-index-url at all requires already knowing it is a substitution risk — that fact comes from Alex Birsan's 2021 research and pip's own documentation, not from anything in requirements.txt itself, so a grep only helps someone who already learned the risk before opening the file. Second, a grep of package.json alone cannot see the interaction that actually matters: an unscoped dependency name is only exposed when .npmrc separately sets a private default registry, and reading one file tells you nothing about the other, so a list of unscoped names by itself does not say which ones, if any, are at risk. Third, there is no single command a developer already runs that checks both ecosystems' configuration shapes together — npm audit and pip's own tooling check known vulnerabilities in packages you depend on, not the shape of your own index and registry configuration. Fourth, a by-hand grep proves nothing afterward: there is no file, line number, or fix to paste into a PR description or an audit trail, only a recollection that someone looked.

QuestionWhere to answer it
I want to search my own requirements.txt for --extra-index-url, and I already know that string is worth searching for.Checking by hand — free, and works once you already know what to search for.
I want every --extra-index-url use across requirements*.txt, constraints*.txt, pip.conf/pip.ini, and my CI workflows found automatically, without knowing in advance which files to check.This tool — scans the standard locations for both, in the browser or the CLI.
I want to know whether an unscoped npm dependency name is actually exposed, which depends on what .npmrc sets.This tool — reads package.json and .npmrc together and only flags a name once a private default registry is in effect.
I want one command that checks both the pip and the npm configuration shape at once, instead of two separate manual searches.This tool's CLI — python3 check.py scans a whole checkout for both patterns in one pass.
I want a report I can paste into a PR description or an audit trail: a file, a line number, the exact match, and the fix.This tool — every finding carries all four; --format json for a machine-readable version.

Checking by hand is not wrong so much as unverifiable: a developer who already knows both patterns, and remembers to check both files together every time either one changes, would eventually catch most of what this tool catches. What it structurally cannot do is teach itself the 2021 research, cross-reference two files it was not told to compare, or leave behind a record that the check happened at all — and this tool's whole design, on both the browser page and the CLI, is built around closing exactly those gaps for free.

This tool needs no account and makes no network calls of its own: the browser page runs entirely client-side and nothing you paste ever leaves your device, and the CLI is a single stdlib-only script that reads files already on disk.

Common questions

What does grepping for --extra-index-url or an unscoped npm name actually catch?

It catches exactly what you already knew to look for. If you already know pip's --extra-index-url can let a second index outbid your private one on version number, a grep for the literal string finds every use in requirements.txt, pip.conf, or a workflow's pip install step. The gap is upstream of the grep: most requirements.txt files that use it were written before dependency confusion was a known risk, so nobody flagged the line as worth searching for in the first place.

Why doesn't grepping package.json for unscoped names tell you anything on its own?

Because an unscoped dependency name is only a dependency-confusion risk in combination with .npmrc setting a private default registry — that is the exact interaction that makes the public registry a fallback for the same name. Reading package.json alone cannot see whether that condition holds, so a list of unscoped names by itself does not tell you which ones, if any, are actually exposed. You would have to check both files together and reason about the interaction yourself, every time either one changes.

Is there a command a developer already runs that checks both patterns together?

No. npm audit and pip's own tooling check known-vulnerability databases against packages you already depend on; neither reads your own .npmrc or requirements.txt for these two configuration shapes, and neither ecosystem's default tooling looks at the other's files at all. A developer who wants both checked has to know to look for both, in both files, and do it by hand — there is no single existing command that already covers this.

Can I put a by-hand grep in a PR description as evidence I checked?

Only as a note that you looked and did not personally notice anything — it names no specific line, no specific finding, and no fix, and there is nothing to attach to a ticket or audit trail besides your own recollection. A structured report with a file, a line number, the exact pattern matched, and the remediation for it is stronger evidence than "I grepped and it looked fine."

Open Dependency Confusion Check to scan your own config, or read what is dependency confusion? for the full mechanism.

← Dependency Confusion Check

This checker vs. Socket

Two different layers: Socket watches your dependency graph and the public registries on an ongoing basis for 70+ risk types, dependency confusion among them. This tool reads the pip/npm configuration you already have, once, locally, for the two specific shapes that make a confusion attack possible — no account, no registry calls, nothing installed.

What each product is for

Socket is a supply-chain security platform. Its own site describes deep package inspection that characterizes what a dependency actually does, rather than relying only on known-vulnerability databases, connected through a GitHub app, a CLI, and a browser extension. It flags more than 70 categories of risk across npm, PyPI, and other ecosystems — dependency confusion, typosquatting, malware, hidden or obfuscated code, risky install scripts, and permission creep among them — and monitors changes to a project's dependency manifest on an ongoing basis. It is free for public, open-source use, and Socket's own site lists paid Team, Business, and Enterprise tiers for private-repository and organization use; today's specific prices and contract terms are not repeated here, since this session cannot verify them live against Socket's own site — only its well-documented product shape is described.

This tool does none of what Socket does. It has no account, no ongoing service, no GitHub app, and no connection of any kind to a package registry — it cannot tell you whether a name is actually published anywhere, let alone whether it behaves maliciously. It reads only the two specific, well-documented configuration shapes behind the 2021 dependency-confusion incidents: a pip --extra-index-url use, and an unscoped npm dependency name while .npmrc sets a private default registry. Paste the files you already have, or run the CLI against a checkout, and get every finding with its fix — free, in your browser or a zero-dependency script, with nothing uploaded and no network calls of its own.

QuestionWhere to answer it

I want a GitHub app or CLI that watches every future pull request for newly introduced risky dependencies.Socket — this tool has no memory between runs and does not watch anything.
I want zero network calls and nothing to install to check a requirements.txt, package.json, and .npmrc I already have.This tool — it never queries a registry, GitHub, or anywhere else.
I want to know whether a specific package name is actually published on the public registry, or has ever shown malicious behavior.Socket — this tool makes no registry calls and cannot answer that.
I want a one-time, local read of the configuration shape itself, split by pattern, with the exact fix.This tool — that is the whole job, and the only one it does.

A team can reasonably run both: Socket for continuous, registry-aware defense against a live attack already under way, and this tool as a fast, zero-account, zero-network first pass over the two specific misconfigurations that make such an attack possible in the first place. This page does not evaluate Socket's detection accuracy and makes no claim about it either way — it only describes Socket's documented product shape and states what this tool does differently. Socket catching a live decoy package and this tool flagging a configuration shape are two different signals; neither replaces the other, and a clean result from either one is not a supply-chain security guarantee.

This tool needs no account and no sign-in: it is a static page, the check runs in your browser (or as a stdlib-only CLI script), and it keeps working with the network connection off.

Common questions

Does Socket check for pip --extra-index-url or an unscoped npm name the same way this tool does?

Not in the way this tool does. Socket's own site describes deep package inspection and real-time monitoring across more than 70 risk categories — including dependency confusion, typosquatting, hidden code, risky install scripts, and permission creep — by watching your dependency graph against live registry data through a GitHub app, CLI, or browser extension. That is package-behavior analysis, not a read of your own requirements.txt, pip.conf, package.json, or .npmrc. This tool does the opposite and narrower thing: it never queries a registry at all, and instead reads those exact files for the two configuration shapes documented in Alex Birsan's 2021 research — a pip --extra-index-url use, and an unscoped npm dependency name behind a private .npmrc registry.

Should I use this tool or Socket?

They work at different layers, and a team can reasonably run both. Socket runs on an ongoing basis against your dependency graph and the public registries, watching for a live attack — a newly published decoy package, a suspicious permission change, or dozens of other package-behavior signals — as a service that is free for public open-source use and offers paid plans for private and organization use, per Socket's own site; connecting it needs a GitHub app, CLI, or browser extension. This tool checks something Socket does not read directly: whether your own pip and npm configuration is shaped so that a confusion attack could work in the first place, entirely on your device, one time, free, no account, no network calls of its own. Socket can catch an attacker who already published a decoy; this tool tells you whether your configuration would fall for one.

what-is-dependency-confusion.html.text:
← Dependency Confusion Check

What is dependency confusion?

Dependency confusion is a supply-chain attack where a package manager installs a public package instead of an organization's internal one of the same name, because the resolver was told about both places the name might live and had no rule saying the internal one always wins.

A real incident

In 2021, researcher Alex Birsan demonstrated this against more than 35 companies — Apple, Microsoft, PayPal, Netflix, Uber, and Tesla among them — by publishing decoy packages under their internal package names on the public npm and PyPI registries. Internal build systems, configured to check the public registry alongside (or instead of) a private one, installed the decoys and executed Birsan's code with real credentials. Some paid out six-figure bug-bounty totals for the finding.

The pip mechanism

pip's own documentation names the risk directly: --extra-index-url tells pip to consider a second index in addition to the primary one, and "the additional repository can specify a version of a package which will be installed instead of the one from index-url." pip compares versions across every configured index and installs whichever reports the higher number for a given name — so a public package published under your internal package's name, at a higher version, wins.

pip install -r requirements.txt --extra-index-url https://pkgs.internal.example.com/simple/

If acme-internal-utils only exists on the internal index today, publishing acme-internal-utils version 999.0.0 on the public PyPI is enough to have pip install the attacker's version everywhere this command runs.

The npm mechanism

npm resolves an unscoped dependency name (no @org/ prefix) against whatever registry is configured for that project — typically set globally in .npmrc with a bare registry= line. That configuration is local to each machine and each CI runner. A developer's laptop with the internal .npmrc resolves an internal package correctly; a CI runner, a new hire's fresh laptop, or an automated dependency-update bot without that file falls back to the public npm registry for the exact same unscoped name — and if nobody has claimed it there, an attacker can.

The fix

  • pip: use --index-url with a single trusted index that proxies or mirrors the public packages you need, instead of --extra-index-url alongside the public index. Most private-index servers (Artifactory, Nexus, a private PyPI mirror) support this. Where that is not possible, pin exact versions with --require-hashes so an unexpected package cannot silently substitute.
  • npm: publish internal packages under an npm org scope (@your-org/package-name) — a scope is bound to your npm org and nobody outside it can publish under it, which removes the ambiguity entirely. Where an unscoped internal name already exists, claim it on the public registry as an empty placeholder so nobody else can.

Check your own configuration

Paste your requirements.txt, pip.conf, package.json, and .npmrc into Dependency Confusion Check to find every --extra-index-url use and unscoped npm name at once, or run the CLI in your own checkout:

python3 check.py --fail-on-risk

That exits with a nonzero status if either pattern is present — wire it into your own CI to block a newly-added one before it merges. Already running a supply-chain platform like Socket? See how this checker differs from Socket — different layers, and worth running both.

No warranty. This page and the tool it describes are provided free and as-is, without warranty of any kind. This is not a security audit or a compliance attestation, and a clean scan does not mean you are not exposed to dependency confusion — only that these two documented patterns were not found.
